# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's a particular moment I find myself thinking about often—that instant when you realize you've taken a wrong turn, when the familiar street signs stop appearing and the landscape tilts toward the unknown. Most people experience a flutter of anxiety in that moment. I understand that reaction. But I've become fascinated by what happens next, in that space between confusion and resolution, where something unexpectedly good often lives.

We're taught from childhood to avoid being lost. Parents give stern instructions. GPS devices promise never to let us astray. We equate being lost with failure, with inefficiency, with a fundamental inability to read a map or pay attention. And yet, some of the most interesting things in my life have happened precisely because I was lost.

There was the afternoon I missed my train station entirely and ended up riding an extra five stops into a neighborhood I'd never visited. Rather than panic, I got off and walked. The streets were tree-lined and quiet. I found a small bookstore I've returned to dozens of times since. The owner knew everyone by name. I met friends there. That single missed stop changed the geography of my regular life in ways I still benefit from.

Or the time I was driving to a dinner party in an unfamiliar city and my phone died. I could have called it quits and turned back. Instead, I drove slowly, followed what seemed like the right general direction, and took a turn that seemed promising. I got slightly lost, yes, but I also discovered a street fair happening that night. I arrived at the dinner party late with stories instead of just myself.

I think we're wrong about what lost really means. We treat it as the opposite of found, as though the world is neatly divided into two categories: places where you're supposed to be and places where you're not. But the world is far messier and more interesting than that. Being lost is simply being in a state of not-yet-knowing. It's a temporary condition, almost always resolvable, and it puts you in a peculiar position of openness.

When you're lost, you have to pay attention. Your usual autopilot is disabled. You notice things. The quality of light on a building. The name of a street. The smell of a bakery you might have driven past a thousand times without seeing. Being lost makes you a tourist in your own geography, and tourism, at its best, is about genuine attention.

There's also something strangely democratic about being lost. It's one of the few remaining universal human experiences. Rich, poor, clever, less so—we all get lost sometimes. I've seen CEOs consulting maps on their phones with the same uncertainty I feel. There's a humility in it. It's a reminder that knowing doesn't extend infinitely in all directions. We're all lost in our own ways, in our own directions, and most of us are trying to figure it out as we go.

The fear of being lost isn't really about geography, I think. It's about control. We want to know where we are. We want to have charted a course and to follow it. Being lost means admitting that the world is larger than our maps, our plans, our understanding. It's admitting that randomness exists and that sometimes you end up places you didn't intend to go.

But here's what I've learned: that's not always bad. Some of the best things are accidents. Every scientific discovery starts with someone noticing something that wasn't on their agenda. Every friendship, every job, every moment of beauty or revelation I can think of came partly through some kind of deviation from the original plan.

I'm not arguing for recklessness or for abandoning all sense of direction. There are contexts where being lost is dangerous, where it matters. But in most of daily life, in most of the low-stakes moments that comprise the bulk of existence, being lost is merely inconvenient. And inconvenience, as I've gotten older, seems like a small price to pay for the possibility of discovery.

There's also something to be said for the productivity of apparent unproductivity. When you're lost, you're not going anywhere. You can't hurry. You have to slow down and actually examine your surroundings, think about where you are, consider your options. In a world that generally rewards speed and efficiency, there's something valuable about being forced into a moment of deliberation. Sometimes those moments clarify things that won't be clarified through rushing.

I've also noticed that the people I find most interesting, most alive in some fundamental way, tend to be comfortable with uncertainty. They navigate it well. They don't pretend to understand things they don't. They explore. They ask questions. They sometimes take the longer route because it seems interesting. They get lost and they don't immediately panic, because they understand that lost is often just another word for "not-yet-arrived."

As I get older, I'm trying to extend this toward the bigger losses, the more existential ones. The career I thought I was going to have that shifted. The person I thought I'd be who turned out differently. The plans that didn't solidify the way I imagined. These are harder. There's a difference between taking a wrong turn on a road and realizing your entire trajectory has been less linear than you'd hoped. But the lesson feels connected somehow. Being lost is also an opportunity. It means something has to change, has to shift, and from that shift comes the possibility of something unexpected.

So I'm trying to make peace with not knowing. I'm trying to learn to navigate uncertainty with the same openness I've learned to navigate unfamiliar streets—with attention, with curiosity, with a willingness to see what's actually in front of me rather than what I'd expected to find. Because most of what's made my life interesting came through deviation, chance, and the peculiar grace of taking wrong turns.

Maybe that's not being lost at all. Maybe it's just moving forward in a world far more complex and surprising than any map can show.
